title: Krishna Protects Draupadi with Endless Robes
story:
In the great assembly hall of Hastinapura, the queen of the Pandavas called out a single name, and her voice filled the silence. It was the only thing she had left. She called on Krishna.

Draupadi had been brought there because her husband Yudhishthira had lost everything at dice. He had staked his kingdom and lost it, staked his brothers and lost them, and then staked himself. And when there was nothing else left to wager, in the madness of the game, he had staked his own wife. Now the court had sent for her, and she stood among the kings and elders who had watched it all happen and said nothing. Only Vidura had spoken against it, warning that the house was calling ruin down on itself, and his warning had been brushed aside.

The messenger had come to her rooms like a dog into a lion's den, as the old text puts it, and told her she had been won, and that she was to be brought before the assembly. Draupadi had answered him with a question no one in the court could answer. When Yudhishthira had nothing left, had he staked himself first, or her? If he had already lost himself, how could he stake anyone at all? The question was carried back to the assembly, and her own husband, the king, sat there like a man demented, and gave no answer, good or ill. He could not say whether he had lost himself before he lost her, and so he said nothing, and his silence hung over the hall like a judgement.

So she was brought before them, and Dussasana laid his hands on her garment and began to pull, to strip her of her honour in front of the whole assembly. The elders looked away. The fathers and grandfathers of the house sat with lowered eyes, and not one of them rose. And Draupadi, alone in that crowded hall, raised her voice and called out to Krishna, pouring out her heart to the one who had never failed her.

Krishna heard her. The text says plainly that, hearing her words, he was deeply moved, and that, leaving his seat, out of compassion he came to her there. He did not thunder, and he did not break down the door. He came the way mercy comes.

And then something the assembly could not explain began to happen. The illustrious Dharma — the very principle of righteousness — remained there unseen, and covered her. As each garment was drawn away, another of the same kind appeared in its place, covering her again. One after another the robes came, without end, of many bright hues, hundreds upon hundreds of them, so that no matter how long Dussasana pulled, Draupadi remained covered. The harder he pulled, the more the robes came, as if the cloth itself had set its mind to keeping her covered. Her honour could not be taken from her.

The pile of cloth rose and rose until Dussasana, spent and disgraced, let go and fell back, and could pull no more. He sank down amid the very heap of robes he had tried to tear from her, and the heap itself stood as a witness against him. Draupadi stood unharmed, wrapped in an endless garment that was not cloth so much as the answer to a prayer. The court sat stunned before the proof of something they had refused to admit.

The protector never showed a face and never spoke a word. But every new robe was a word, and together they said what no one in that hall had been willing to say: the woman who calls on Krishna is never left alone.
reflection: The text does not say Krishna struck anyone or even raised his voice; it says he was moved, and that the unseen Dharma covered her. The miracle is a quiet one — not a display of power but an answer to a call, given so that honour and dignity could not be torn away.
content_note: Describes the attempted public humiliation of Draupadi, whose garment is seized before the assembly; the scene is handled with restraint, and she is protected.
hero_scene: Draupadi standing in the crowded Kuru assembly, calling out to Krishna as Dussasana pulls at her garment, while robe after robe of many hues appears around her, covering her again and again, the elders looking on in silence.
visual_elements: Draupadi calling out with raised hands
endless many-hued robes appearing one after another
the silent elders of the Kuru court
the great assembly hall of Hastinapura
